q: Users, payments and the links between them, with multi-row transactions. Default store?
options: A document store such as MongoDB
A wide-column store such as Cassandra
A relational database such as Postgres
why: Joins, foreign keys and ACID transactions are what relational databases are for. Pick something else only when you can name the access pattern Postgres cannot serve.

q: 500k sensor writes per second, always read back by device and time range. Best fit?
options: One Postgres primary with a B-tree index on timestamp
A wide-column store (Cassandra, DynamoDB) keyed by (device_id, day)
why: Partitioning by device and day spreads writes across nodes and keeps each range query on one partition. A single relational primary cannot absorb 500k writes/s.

q: Officers need fuzzy, ranked search across 50M documents. What do you add?
options: A search index (OpenSearch / Elasticsearch) fed from the primary DB
A Redis cache of every document
why: An inverted index makes term lookups fast and supports ranking. LIKE '%term%' cannot use a B-tree index, so it scans the whole table.

q: Citizens upload 5 MB PDFs with their applications. Where do the bytes go?
options: On the API server's local disk
Object storage (S3); the DB keeps the key, size, owner and scan status
why: Object storage is cheap, durable and serves large files without tying up DB connections or memory. Local disk is lost when the instance is replaced.

q: Cache-aside. You just updated a row in the DB. What do you do with the cache?
options: Write the new value into the cache before the DB
Nothing, the TTL will handle it
Delete the key, so the next read loads the fresh row
why: Deleting after the DB commit is simple and avoids a race where two writers set the cache in the wrong order. Keep a TTL as a safety net for any delete that is lost.

q: A hot key expires and 5,000 requests miss at once, all hitting the DB. Fix?
options: Request coalescing: one request rebuilds the value while the others wait or get the stale copy
Add another read replica and hope
Switch eviction from LRU to LFU
why: This is a cache stampede. Single-flight locking, serving stale while refreshing, or refreshing early before expiry all keep the DB to one rebuild.

q: Which write policy can lose writes the client was told succeeded if the cache node dies?
why: Write-back acknowledges after writing only to the cache and flushes to the DB later. Anything not yet flushed is lost with the node.

q: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
options: To make the cache harder to attack
To improve the LRU hit rate
Because TTLs must be prime numbers
So keys loaded together do not all expire in the same second
why: Keys warmed together expire together and stampede the DB together. A TTL of 600 s plus or minus 60 s spreads the reloads out.

q: A link shortener must count every click. Which redirect status?
options: 302 (or 307), so every click comes back to your server
why: Browsers cache a 301 permanently, so repeat clicks never reach you and your counts go low. You also cannot re-point a link once it is cached.

q: Which set of methods is idempotent by the HTTP spec?
why: Repeating a PUT or DELETE leaves the same state. POST is not idempotent, which is why it needs an idempotency key when clients retry.

q: A payment POST times out and the client retries. How do you avoid charging twice?
options: The client sends an Idempotency-Key; the server stores it with the result under a unique constraint and replays that result on retry
Check whether a payment with the same amount arrived in the last minute
why: The key turns a retry into a lookup. Matching on amount and time blocks real repeat payments and still misses slow retries.

q: Processing an uploaded CSV takes 3 minutes. What should POST /upload return?
options: Hold the connection open for 3 minutes and return 200
504 and ask the user to retry
202 Accepted with a job id; the client polls GET /jobs/{id} or gets a callback
why: Long requests hit load balancer and gateway timeouts and tie up workers. This is the long-running-upload follow-up in GovTech's ACE take-home.

q: A client is over its rate limit. What do you return?
options: 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
why: 429 tells the client it is being throttled, not refused, and Retry-After tells well-behaved clients when to come back.

q: Your queue delivers at least once. What must the consumer do?
options: Nothing, at least once means no duplicates
Be idempotent, for example dedupe on a message id or use an upsert
Process each message twice to be safe
why: At least once means a message can arrive again after a crash or visibility timeout. Acking before processing turns it into at most once and loses messages.

q: A vendor promises exactly-once delivery end to end. What is actually achievable?
options: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which gives an effectively-once result
True exactly-once over any network with the right broker
Exactly-once only if you use TCP
why: A sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost ack, so it must resend. Kafka's exactly-once covers read-process-write inside Kafka; side effects such as emails still need dedupe.

q: Events for one user must be processed in order, using Kafka with 24 partitions. How?
options: Use one partition for the whole topic
Sort events by timestamp in the consumer
why: Kafka orders messages only within a partition. Keying by user keeps each user's events in order and still spreads users across 24 partitions.

q: A service saves an order and must publish OrderCreated. The DB commit succeeds, then the publish fails. Fix?
options: Publish first, then write to the DB
Wrap the DB and the broker in a two-phase commit
Transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it
Retry the publish in the request thread until it works
why: One local transaction makes the order and its event commit or fail together. The relay may publish twice, so consumers stay idempotent.

q: A booking spans payment, slot reservation and notification services, each with its own DB. How do you keep them consistent?
options: One distributed ACID transaction across all three
A saga: local steps with compensating actions (refund, release slot) on failure
Put all three tables in one shared DB
why: Sagas give eventual consistency without holding locks across services. Each step must have an undo that is safe to run more than once.

q: One malformed message fails 5 times and blocks the consumer. What do you do?
options: Move it to a dead-letter queue, alert, and keep processing the rest
why: A poison message must not stall the queue. The DLQ keeps it for inspection and replay once the bug is fixed.

q: Audit, analytics and notifications must each see every event, and you want to replay last week. What do you use?
options: One SQS queue shared by all three
Direct HTTP calls from the producer
A log/stream (Kafka, Kinesis) with one consumer group per service
why: A shared queue hands each message to only one consumer and deletes it on ack. A log keeps events for a retention period, and each group tracks its own offset.

q: Producers send 5k msg/s and consumers handle 2k msg/s for a 10-minute spike. Backlog at the end?
why: (5,000 - 2,000) × 600 s = 1.8M. At 2k/s with no new load that is 15 minutes to drain, so add consumers or accept the delay.

q: An account with 50M followers posts. Fan-out on write would mean 50M inserts. What do big feed systems do?
options: A hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull celebrity posts at read time
Pull everything at read time for everyone
Only show the post to online followers
why: Fan-out on write makes reads cheap but explodes for huge accounts. Merging a few celebrity posts in at read time caps the write cost.

q: Searching nearby drivers by geohash prefix, why also query the 8 neighbouring cells?
options: A driver 50 m away can sit across a cell edge with a different prefix
To get more results for ranking
why: Points close together can have different prefixes at a boundary. Query the cell plus its 8 neighbours, then filter by real distance.

q: Roughly how big is a geohash cell of length 6?
why: Length 5 is about 4.9 km square, 6 is about 1.2 × 0.6 km and 7 is about 153 m square. Pick the length whose cell matches your search radius.

q: 100k drivers each send a location every 4 seconds. Where do the live positions go?
options: One INSERT per update into Postgres
An in-memory geo index (Redis GEO) that keeps only the latest point per driver
A search index rebuilt every minute
why: That is 25k writes/s of data that is stale in 4 seconds. Keep the latest point in memory, and stream history to cheap storage if you need it.

q: N = 3 replicas. Which (W, R) guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write?
why: You need R + W > N, so every read set overlaps every write set. 2 + 2 = 4 > 3; the other options sum to 3 or less.

q: How many Raft nodes do you need to survive 2 crashed nodes?
why: Raft needs a majority, so tolerating f crash failures takes 2f + 1 nodes. With 5 nodes, 3 survivors still form a majority.

q: Nodes may lie, not just crash (Byzantine faults). How many nodes does PBFT need to tolerate f of them?
why: Byzantine agreement needs 3f + 1 nodes; crash-only consensus such as Raft needs 2f + 1. Worth naming if the "chain of consensus" prompt (reported, unverified, one line with no spec) turns to untrusted parties.

q: How does Raft stop an old leader from committing writes after a new one is elected?
options: The load balancer routes away from it
Terms and majorities: the old leader cannot get a majority to ack, and higher terms make it step down
Clients pick the leader with the newest timestamp
why: An entry commits only when a majority stores it in the current term. A partitioned old leader can accept writes but never commit them.

q: A client holding a lock pauses for 30 s during GC, the lock expires, and then it writes. How do you stop the stale write?
options: Fencing tokens: the lock service hands out an increasing number and storage rejects lower ones
why: A pause can always outlast a TTL. Only the storage side can reject the stale writer, by comparing tokens.

q: A partition splits the cluster. Account balances must never be shown stale. What do you choose?
options: Consistency: the minority side refuses or errors until the partition heals (CP)
Availability: serve the last known balance (AP)
Neither: shut the whole system down
why: During a partition you can either answer with possibly stale data or refuse. For money, refusing is safer than a wrong balance.

q: What does PACELC add to CAP?
options: A third choice besides C and A during a partition
That partitions never happen in one region
Even with no partition, you trade latency against consistency
why: Synchronous replication to a quorum costs round trips on every write. Many systems pick lower latency (EL) in normal operation.

q: A user updates their profile, reloads, and sees the old value. Reads go to replicas. Fix?
options: Read-your-writes: send that user's reads to the primary for a short window, or wait until the replica reaches their write's position
Ask the user to wait and refresh
why: Async replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds. Route only the writer's own reads to the primary; everyone else can read slightly stale data.

q: The primary fails under async replication. What can you lose?
options: Writes that were acknowledged but not yet copied to the promoted replica
why: Async replication acks before the replica has the write. Semi-sync, or a quorum, bounds the loss at the cost of write latency.

q: The DB is CPU-bound on writes. Will read replicas help?
options: No. Every replica replays every write; you need batching, a write-optimised store or sharding
Yes, replicas share the write load
Yes, if you add at least three
why: Replicas scale reads. Write throughput is capped by the primary, and every replica does the same writes again.

q: A multi-agency SaaS where almost every query is within one agency. Shard key?
options: agency_id, with a plan to split very large agencies
why: Sharding on the tenant keeps each query on one shard. Watch for one huge tenant becoming a hot shard.

q: One short link gets 50k requests/s and its shard is overloaded. Fix?
options: Cache the hot key in front of its shard (an in-process cache on each app server, or Redis replicas)
Rate limit the people clicking the link
why: A hot key is skew that re-sharding cannot fix: the key still lands on one shard. Serve it from caches in front of the shard. A CDN can also cache the redirect, but then you must count clicks from edge logs. For a hot counter, split it into N sub-counters and sum them.

q: You shard by created_at ranges. What goes wrong?
options: All new writes land on the newest shard
Rows get lost at shard boundaries
why: Time is monotonic, so the latest range takes all the inserts. Hash on a key, or combine a key with time.

q: With hash(key) % N, N goes from 4 to 5. About what fraction of keys move?
why: A key stays put only if hash % 4 equals hash % 5, which is about 1 key in 5. That mass move is why consistent hashing exists.

q: A consistent hash ring has 4 nodes with vnodes. You add a 5th. About what fraction of keys move?
why: The new node takes an equal share from the others, so only about 1/N of keys move. Virtual nodes keep that share even.

q: You want to allow short bursts but cap the sustained rate. Which algorithm?
why: Bucket capacity sets the burst and refill rate sets the sustained limit. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate instead.

q: Fixed window, limit 100 per minute. What is the worst case?
options: About 200 requests in 2 seconds around a window boundary
It blocks everyone at the boundary
why: 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00 both pass. A sliding window counter weights the previous window to smooth this out.

q: Ten API servers must share one limit per user. Where do the counters live?
options: In Redis, updated atomically (INCR with expiry, or a Lua script)
In the Postgres primary, one UPDATE per request
why: Per-server memory gives each user 10× the limit. Redis adds well under a millisecond in the same AZ, and atomic ops avoid races.

q: A dashboard that only receives server updates every few seconds and must pass through corporate proxies. Transport?
why: SSE is one-way, runs over plain HTTP, reconnects automatically and passes proxies easily. Use WebSockets when the client also streams to the server.

q: A chat with low-latency messages in both directions. Transport?
why: One long-lived, full-duplex connection per client. Plan for sticky connections and for routing a message to whichever server holds the recipient's socket.

q: A few hundred users check a job's status, which changes about once a minute. Simplest correct choice?
options: SSE through a dedicated push service
why: Hundreds of cheap GETs per minute is nothing. Do not add stateful connections you have to scale and monitor.

q: User A's socket is on server 1 and user B's is on server 7. How does A's message reach B?
options: Servers publish to a shared pub/sub channel (or look up B's server in a registry) and server 7 pushes to B
Server 1 opens a socket straight to B
The load balancer copies every message to every server
why: Socket servers are stateful. Redis pub/sub, or a user-to-server registry plus internal RPC, connects them.

q: Users upload 200 MB files. How do you keep the API servers out of the data path?
options: Stream the file through the API server
Base64 it into a JSON body
Raise the API's body size limit to 500 MB
Issue a short-lived presigned PUT URL; the client uploads straight to object storage
why: The API only signs a URL valid for a few minutes for one key. Confirm afterwards with an upload event, then virus-scan before marking the file usable.

q: Which of these is a poor fit for CDN caching?
options: A signed-in user's account page with their balance
why: Per-user responses must not be shared from an edge cache. Send Cache-Control: private, no-store on them.

q: You deploy a new app.js. How do users get it without waiting for CDN TTLs?
options: Purge the whole CDN on every deploy
Put a content hash in the filename (app.3f9a1c.js) and cache it for a year
Set TTL to 0 on all assets
why: A new hash is a new URL, so there is nothing to invalidate. Only the small HTML file that references it needs a short TTL.

q: 1M daily users × 10 requests each. Average requests per second?
why: 10M / 86,400 s ≈ 116/s. Quote peak as 2-3× that. A day is about 10^5 seconds; that shortcut is enough.

q: 100M new rows a day at 500 bytes each, kept 5 years. Raw storage?
why: 100M × 500 B = 50 GB/day; × 365 × 5 ≈ 91 TB, before indexes and replicas (often 2-3× more).

q: go.gov.sg reported 190M clicks in Q3 2026, about 2.1M a day. Rough peak redirect rate at 3× average?
why: 190M / 92 days ≈ 2.1M/day; 2.1M / 86,400 ≈ 24/s; × 3 ≈ 73/s. Its public README describes a Postgres primary, a read replica for redirects and Redis for hot links, which handles that easily, so do not open with sharding.

q: How many 7-character base62 codes are there?
why: 62^7 ≈ 3.52 × 10^12. Even at 10M new links a day that lasts about 1,000 years.

q: A downstream call fails intermittently. How should clients retry?
options: Exponential backoff with jitter and a retry cap
why: Jitter stops every client retrying in lockstep and making the outage worse. Only retry idempotent calls, or calls sent with an idempotency key.

q: A dependency is down and every call waits 30 s to time out, using up your threads. What helps?
options: A circuit breaker that fails fast, plus a short timeout
why: After N failures the breaker opens and fails calls at once, then lets a trial request through to test recovery. That stops one dead dependency from taking down your service.

q: Two services in series, each 99.9% available. Combined availability?
why: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998. Serial dependencies multiply; redundant parallel copies are how you claw availability back.

q: How much downtime does a 99.9% monthly SLO allow?
why: 0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43.2 minutes. 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes, which in practice means no manual steps in recovery.

q: Your app needs a signed statement of who the user is after login. Which standard gives you that?
options: OpenID Connect, via its ID token
why: OAuth 2.0 is for authorization: a token to call an API on the user's behalf. OIDC adds an ID token (a signed JWT) about the authenticated user.

q: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked server-side. What is the usual fix?
options: Put the password hash in the token
Rotate the signing key on every logout
Short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) plus refresh tokens checked against a store you can revoke
why: A short expiry bounds the damage. A refresh-token store, or a denylist of jti values for urgent cases, gives you a revoke button.

q: You store NRIC numbers and must look them up by exact match. Best approach?
options: Store a plain SHA-256 hash only
Store it in plaintext behind a firewall
Encrypt the field (KMS envelope encryption) and store a keyed HMAC of it as a lookup index
why: The NRIC space is tiny: a few prefix letters × 10^7 digits, and the check letter is computed from them. That is under 10^8 values, so an unkeyed hash falls to brute force in seconds. A keyed HMAC resists that, and encryption keeps the value recoverable for people with the key.

q: Why must an OTP verify endpoint cap attempts?
options: A 6-digit code has only 10^6 values; without a cap it can be brute-forced
So the SMS bill stays low
why: With 5 attempts per code the guess chance is 5 in a million. Also expire codes in a few minutes, store them hashed, and rate limit per phone number and IP.

q: How does a receiver check that a webhook really came from you and is not a replay?
options: Sign the body plus a timestamp (HMAC or ed25519) and reject old timestamps
Send it over HTTPS, that is enough
Include a static shared secret in the URL
why: The signature proves origin and integrity; the timestamp window stops replays. FormSG's webhooks, for example, are signed with ed25519 and allow 5 minutes of clock tolerance.

q: An officer from agency A calls GET /forms/123, which belongs to agency B. The ID is valid. What happens?
options: Return the form, the user is logged in
Rely on the UI hiding the link
Return it but log a warning
The server checks ownership on every request and returns 403 or 404
why: This is an IDOR (broken object-level authorization). Authentication says who you are; each object access still needs an authorization check.
